title_en: Rail Strike Called Off at the Eleventh Hour
title_ru: Забастовка на железной дороге отменена в последний момент
description_ru: Вымышленная новость о том, как переговоры накануне забастовки на железной дороге Нортвейл завершились соглашением, и что это значит для пассажиров.
text:
NORTHVALE - A nationwide rail strike that threatened to paralyse the country for five days was called off shortly before midnight on Sunday, after union leaders and the operator of the Northvale network reached a tentative agreement at the end of a marathon negotiation that lasted almost thirty hours.

Trains will therefore run as normal from Monday morning, bringing relief to commuters, students, holidaymakers and thousands of businesses that had been preparing for severe disruption. Station staff began removing warning posters at about one in the morning, and by dawn the first services were leaving on schedule.

The dispute, which began six months ago, centred on pay, working hours and plans to close about two hundred ticket offices. The union, which represents more than twenty-five thousand drivers, signallers and station workers, had demanded an increase of eight per cent to compensate for the rising cost of living, while the operator had offered four and insisted that any more would force it to raise fares or cut services. Both sides had repeatedly accused the other of intransigence, and two previous rounds of talks had ended in recrimination.

The breakthrough came, according to people close to the negotiations, after the government's transport secretary, Marcus Whitlow, agreed to join the talks on Saturday evening. Although ministers have repeatedly insisted that the dispute is a matter for employers and unions, Mr Whitlow is understood to have offered a one-off grant to support a pay rise, in return for assurances that the operator would carry out its reforms more gradually. "Everyone had run out of road," said one participant who asked not to be named. "The only way forward was for somebody to blink."

Details of the agreement have not been published, and both sides have stressed that it must be approved in a vote of union members, which is expected within three weeks. However, leaked briefing notes suggest that staff will receive a rise of six per cent this year and a further three the next, backdated to the start of April, together with a guarantee that no worker will be dismissed because of the ticket-office closures. The proposals to shut the ticket offices, meanwhile, are to be reviewed by an independent panel, which will include representatives of disabled passengers.

The general secretary of the union, Dolores Quinlan, who looked visibly exhausted as she emerged from the talks, was cautious in her comments. "I am not going to claim victory," she told reporters. "What we have is an offer that we believe is worth putting to our members, and I will be recommending it. Nobody takes industrial action lightly. Our members lose wages when they strike, and they know that passengers suffer. But they have also seen their living standards fall, and they wanted to be heard."

The operator's chief executive, Alistair Penhaligon, acknowledged that the company had made concessions, but he insisted that the outcome would not be paid for by passengers. "This is a fair settlement that recognises the work our staff do every day," he said. "We have been clear throughout that we would not allow ourselves to be pushed into a deal that would result in higher fares, and I can confirm that this agreement will not." Some analysts doubted that claim. Imogen Haldane, an economist at a transport think tank, said that the finances of the network were already precarious and that the additional cost would have to come from somewhere. "It is difficult to see how six per cent plus three per cent is paid for without either more public money or some change in fares," she said. "Someone will foot the bill, and it may well be the taxpayer."

Reaction among passengers was understandably mixed. At Northvale Central, the busiest station in the country, a nurse called Tamsin Okoro said that she was thrilled because she depended on the first morning service to reach her hospital shift. "I could not have walked twelve miles," she said, laughing. "I understand why they wanted to strike, honestly I do, but it feels like we are always the ones in the middle." A student nearby was less forgiving. "I have already lost two weeks of lectures to the previous strikes," he said, "and I would like to know why it takes thirty hours of talks to do what should have taken three days."

Business groups, who had calculated that the stoppage would cost the economy roughly four hundred million pounds, welcomed the news with obvious relief but warned that the dispute exposed deeper problems. "This cannot be allowed to happen again," said the director of a major retail association. "We need a system in which disagreements are resolved long before the eleventh hour, because on this occasion we were only saved by a few hours."

Not all the union's members are certain to endorse the proposal. A group of drivers in the north of the country has already circulated a statement criticising the deal as insufficient, and there was a fierce argument at a branch meeting on Sunday night. Ms Quinlan acknowledged the dissent, but she expressed confidence that the proposal would pass. If it does not, she added, the threat of further action would return immediately.

For the moment, however, the departure boards at Northvale Central glowed with unremarkable normality. As the first train of the day pulled out at six minutes past five, the driver sounded the horn and, according to a witness, received a small cheer from the otherwise deserted platform.

questions.question: What was the strike about?
questions.answer: Pay, working hours and plans to close ticket offices.

questions.question: What helped to break the deadlock?
questions.answer: The transport secretary joined the talks and offered a grant.

questions.question: What pay rise is reported in the leaked notes?
questions.answer: Six per cent this year and three per cent next year.

questions.question: What must happen before the deal is final?
questions.answer: Union members must vote to approve it.
